The Perfect Shoe

Concept to prototype · Rev. 2

Everything I look for in a basketball shoe, combined into one: ankle support, comfort, traction and protection when I jump. I started with the needs of the athlete, then took the shoe from concept to a printed prototype, choosing every material and construction method for performance. Click any part of the shoe to see why it looks the way it does.

Behind the design

How the shoe went from athlete needs to a concept, a printed prototype and testing, with materials, construction and how it would be manufactured in mind at each step.

Materials

Picked for performance

  • Filon upper for breathability and durability, with a TPU net for strength at almost no weight
  • Carbon fiber plate for energy return, weighed against stiffness and weight
  • Next: recycled rubber and TPU to make the build more sustainable
Development

Concept to prototype

  • Took the shoe from athlete research to concept, CAD and a printed prototype
  • Designed it as four parts that assemble into one shoe
  • Iterated the design from a low/mid cut to a high-top
Testing

Built on athlete input

  • Surveyed players and coaches to set the requirements
  • Compared the shoes I've played in to find what to keep
  • Next: traction, plate flex, heel slip and wear testing
Engineering

Making it work

  • Built the model from a parametric Fusion 360 script so the design can change and regenerate
  • Solved for printability: 2.4 mm one-piece upper walls
  • Kept manufacturing in mind: a cupsole, a stitched strobel and a plate that could be produced at scale and on cost

Printed

I printed the first version of the shoe on an Ultimaker as four separate parts: the upper, the carbon plate, the strobel with its pods, and the cupsole. They stack together into one shoe.

Data

The design is based on field research rather than personal preference. I surveyed players and coaches, consulted footwear engineers, and wear-tested current performance models to set the requirements.

Surveys

Player and coach surveys on fit, cut height, traction and ankle support defined the core requirements.

Interviews

Conversations with coaches and players identified the most common on-court failure points: ankle rolls, lost traction and wear.

Industry mentors

Design reviews with footwear designers and engineers at Nike and Adidas on materials and construction.

Wear-testing

Side-by-side comparison of the Dame 6, Kobe 6, GT Cut, PG 6 and Melo 0.1.

References

I took the best feature of each shoe I've worn or studied, and left out the ones that worked against ankle support and protection.

If I started today

I started this project four years ago. Since then, footwear technology has moved fast. Here is what I would change now, mostly inspired by Nike products, along with ideas from other brands.

01 · Cushioning

A ZoomX core

Inspired by G.T. Cut 3 · 2024
Then

The base is a thin layer of React foam, with most of the cushioning coming from the full-length Zoom strobel and carbon plate. A thick layer of foam on top of a strobel would have made the shoe too heavy.

Now

The G.T. Cut 3 brought ZoomX foam to a basketball shoe for the first time. ZoomX is lighter and more responsive, so I could pair it with my full-length Zoom strobel for more energy return without the weight I was worried about.

02 · Materials

React to ReactX

Inspired by ReactX · 2023
Then

The base of the shoe is Nike React foam. I chose it for performance only. Sustainability wasn't part of my requirements.

Now

ReactX is injection molded instead of compression molded, cutting the midsole's carbon footprint by at least 43% while adding 13% more energy return than React. Swapping React for ReactX is a direct upgrade: better performance and a lower carbon footprint, and sustainability becomes a requirement from day one.

03 · Upper

A honeycomb TPU cage

Inspired by adidas AE 1 · 2024
Then

The TPU net is a band laid over the Filon upper. It adds strength, but it doesn't really hold the foot in place.

Now

The AE 1 wraps the upper in a honeycomb-shaped TPU piece that is strong enough to give the shoe structure and containment, but soft enough to conform to the foot. I would turn my TPU net into a molded honeycomb cage that wraps the midfoot and connects to the heel lock, for better lockdown on hard cuts without a heavy overlay.

04 · Traction

Test a lighter sole

Inspired by Under Armour Flow · Curry Flow line
Then

The outsole is full rubber with the Dame 6-style herringbone, because traction was the one thing I would not give up.

Now

Under Armour's Curry Flow shoes use a rubberless sole: the foam itself grips the court, saving two to three ounces and adding court feel. I would keep the herringbone pattern but test a Flow-style foam outsole against rubber on a dusty court, and only switch if it holds the same grip.

05 · Cost

Built to mass produce

Inspired by G.T. Cut Academy
Then

I put every technology I liked into one shoe: a full-length Zoom strobel, a carbon fiber plate, React foam, a TPU net and a rubber heel counter.

Now

Packing all of that into one shoe is unrealistic to mass produce at a price that still makes a profit. Nike solves this with tiers: the G.T. Cut Academy keeps the G.T. Cut look and traction but swaps in Renew foam and a small forefoot Zoom unit to land under $100. I would do the same: keep the Zoom strobel and traction that define the shoe, and cut or shrink the parts that cost the most, starting with a shorter plate and a TPU net only where the upper takes load.

Could it sell?

The shoe modeled at Nike scale: a Vietnam factory, a $160 retail price, 2024 to 2027. Change how well it sells or the price and watch the numbers move.
